author: pkowalczuk
message:
> This probably doesn’t happen often, but it’s prone to name collisions.

From godoc: The provided key must be comparable and should not be of type string or any other built-in type to avoid collisions between packages using context. Users of WithValue should define their own types for keys. To avoid allocating when assigning to an interface{}, context keys often have concrete type struct{}. Alternatively, exported context key variables' static type should be a pointer or interface.

author: Chris Branch
message:
For an idea of how "context" (as used for storing ctx.Value) might appear if given language support, look at Racket and its continuation marks. It's essentially an implicit, globally-available version of "context".

The fact that nobody has been in a hurry to reimplement that in the 15 years since the technique was developed may suggest it's not ergonomically worthwhile unless you have a genuine technical reason (i.e. supporting call/cc)

author: korya
message:
I disagree with you that the only problem context.Context solves is cancellation. Yes, this is probably the main problem that it solves in most of the cases, but not the only one. As its name suggests it provides a context for some execution/calculation. A logical run-time context for an execution.

We use very context's WithValue() very intensively in order to provide some default app service registry. Then later by adding couple decorators/middleware calls we can in run-time reconfigure this app service per API call. For example, in order to diagnose some specific case I can pass a flag and a standard logger will be replaced with a more verbose one that will redirect all the output to a certain location so I can get an immediate feedback. Another example is to use it as backbone for feature flags or A/B testing.

It is a very simple concept, and very explicit so there is no magic. IMHO the 2 main problems with context.Context that it is too low-level and it is a run-time feature.

EDIT: the nice part of having context.Value is that the same "context-aware" API, your API, can be easily used with a lot of user interfaces: HTTP REST endpoints, CLI utilities and GUI. Just make sure to configure the context and pass it to your API. The main problem though is that it is a run-time feature, and there is no way to statically validate that the API contract is obeyed and context.Context is configured as expected by the latter.

PS I am not arguing that this is most elegant and essential feature of Go. There are other ways to solve the problems I described above. But what I am trying to say is that there is a valid use case for context.WithValue
